title: The HN canon
pitch: The ten videos Hacker News has pointed people to most often, thread after thread and year after year. Math, money, programming, chips, biology and how to live, all in one place.
intro: If you only watch ten things from this collection, make it these. Each one has been recommended by many different HN commenters over many years, across every kind of thread, not just programming ones. The list opens with short, easy pieces and works up to the longer lectures, closing with the talk HN sends people when life gets hard.

videos.note: A four-minute start: Rosling animates two centuries of health and wealth, and HN keeps sharing it as a short antidote to cynicism.
The highest-scoring video in the whole collection, and the opening chapter of the series HN credits with finally making linear algebra click.
Fifteen minutes and three stories about connecting the dots, losing Apple and death, sent on HN for years to graduates and anyone at a career crossroads.
Recommended by more HN commenters than any other video here, as the best plain-language explanation of credit, debt and economic cycles.
Technology Connections at its best: half an hour on dishwashers that a surprising number of HN readers say changed how they run theirs.
Patrick Winston's MIT lecture on giving talks, which HN treats as the one lecture on presenting everyone should see, with commenters urging you to drop what you're doing and watch it.
Jim Weirich live-codes his way to the Y combinator, and HN calls it perhaps the most entertaining technical talk ever given.
HN's favorite in-depth introduction to how chips are actually made, from lithography to clean rooms, and a reliable source of awe.
Richard Hamming draws on his Bell Labs years for career advice on choosing important problems, which HN has passed around for over a decade.
A fitting close: Pausch's lecture on childhood dreams, given while he was dying of cancer, which HN still recommends to anyone facing setbacks.

title: Talks every programmer should watch
pitch: The programming talks Hacker News tells every developer to watch, whatever language they write. Simplicity, design, craft and how to think about software.
intro: These are the talks that turn up in thread after thread when someone asks what every programmer should see. None of them is a language tutorial. The list starts with Rich Hickey's Simple Made Easy, then moves through design and APIs, everyday code craft and testing, ways of thinking, and working with other people. It ends with two wider looks at the state of software.

videos.note: The place to start: Hickey's split between simple (not intertwined) and easy (familiar) gives you a vocabulary for complexity that the rest of this list keeps using, and HN calls it a must-watch even if you never touch Clojure.
Ousterhout's hour on deep modules and managing complexity is HN's standard short version of his book, and a practical companion to Hickey's ideas.
Joshua Bloch treats every programmer as an occasional API designer, and HN has called this the best resource on the subject since 2011.
Moving from design to the code itself, Metz refactors a tangle of conditionals into small objects and explains why duplication is cheaper than the wrong abstraction.
A short talk on shaping your data so that whole classes of bugs cannot happen; the examples are in Elm, but HN commenters say the ideas carry over to any typed language.
The talk that introduced 'functional core, imperative shell', which HN recommends as a practical answer to how to test code without mocking everything.
Cooper goes back to Kent Beck's original idea of testing behaviour rather than implementation details, and many commenters say it changed how they write tests.
From code to thinking: Hickey's case for stepping away from the keyboard and letting your background mind solve the problem, which HN treats as permission to think before you type.
Victor's live demos of tools that show results as you type, plus his argument for organising your work around a principle, left one commenter writing that it blew their mind.
Steele makes his point about extensible languages by giving the talk in one-syllable words plus terms he defines as he goes, and HN calls it perhaps the best talk ever on the topic.
Software is a team sport: Fitzpatrick and Collins-Sussman make the case for humility, code review and sharing work early, and HN readers call it career-shaping.
Erlang's co-creator gives a funny, opinionated tour of why software got so tangled, which HN still finds accurate years later.
The widest view to end on: Blow argues that knowledge gets lost between generations and that software quality is already slipping, and his talk is the usual link in HN threads on software decay.

title: Computers from the transistor up
pitch: How a computer works, one layer at a time: transistors and logic gates, how chips get made, CPUs and memory, the operating system, and finally compilers and languages.
intro: A bottom-up path through the whole machine, made of the explainers and talks Hacker News keeps pointing people to. It opens with Feynman's plain-language picture of what a computer is, then climbs from a single transistor through logic, chip fabrication, a working CPU, memory and caches, the operating system, and ends with lexers, compilers and an interpreter. Watch in order; each video assumes roughly what the ones before it covered.

videos.note: The welcoming opener: Feynman builds a computer out of a very dumb, very fast filing clerk, the picture to keep in mind for every layer that follows.
The bottom layer, in eleven minutes: Ben Eater explains what a transistor actually does, and HN calls it the most enlightening starting point.
One step up, Eater wires transistors into logic gates, the moment switches turn into something that can compute.
How billions of those transistors get onto a chip; HN repeatedly calls this HOPE talk the best in-depth introduction to IC manufacturing for any background.
Going the other way, from die photos back to a transistor-level simulation, shows what a real CPU looks like as a physical layout of gates.
That same 6502 on a breadboard: Eater gets a working computer to say hello, which HN calls the best hands-on way to understand a CPU from first principles.
Branch Education's animated tour of DRAM, from capacitor cells to how memory talks to the CPU, praised on HN for being detailed and still easy to follow.
Between the CPU and that memory sit the caches, and Scott Meyers shows why they quietly decide how fast real programs run.
Up to the operating system: Kernighan, Thompson and Ritchie explain the kernel, the shell and pipes in a 1982 Bell Labs film HN calls incredibly clear.
Liz Rice live-codes a container in a few lines of Go, a hands-on look at the kernel features (namespaces, cgroups) a modern OS gives programs.
The first step of any compiler, turning text into tokens, explained so elegantly by Rob Pike that HN says it is easy to follow with no parsing background.
Matt Godbolt shows the assembly a compiler actually produces, tying the language layer back down to the CPU instructions from earlier in the list.
The top of the stack: a Lisp interpreter written in Lisp, a fitting close where a language ends up describing itself.

title: Learn deep learning from zero
pitch: A learning path from 'what is a neuron' to building GPT in code, using the explainers HN recommends most at each step.
intro: A study plan for programmers who want to understand modern language models properly. It starts with visual intuition, moves to building backprop and a convnet by hand, covers why transformers replaced RNNs, and finishes with building and using GPT-style models. Each video assumes you have watched the ones before it. Plan for about 15 hours, and the from-scratch lectures are worth coding along with.

videos.note: HN's default first stop, with 16 recommenders: neurons, layers and digit recognition as animation, no code yet.
The first of Welch Labs' very short videos that turn the picture into a working Python network, which an HN commenter called one of the clearest walkthroughs online.
The step where backprop stops being magic, because you build a tiny autograd engine yourself, and HN's top-scored video in machine learning.
Two practical hours on MNIST and convnets that cover what textbooks skip: why networks fail to train and how to fix them.
Leo Dirac covers bag of words, RNNs and LSTMs, then attention, so you know what problem transformers solved before you meet them.
Yannic Kilcher reads the original transformer paper with you, a good point to see the source before the polished explanations.
The visual version of the paper, which many HN commenters say is where embeddings and attention finally clicked.
The capstone build: a GPT in PyTorch in two hours, which 14 HN commenters call the best video on the topic.
After building one model, step back to scaling laws and the compute-efficient frontier that every model seems to run up against.
Sasha Rush on the main alternative to attention, so you finish knowing where the architecture debate is heading.
The practical close: Jeremy Howard on using, prompting and fine-tuning the models you now understand from the inside.

title: Programming history in 12 talks
pitch: The story of programming in the talks and films Hacker News recommends, from wartime codebreaking machines through Unix, PARC, the home computer boom, free software and the web.
intro: A chronological walk through programming history, told mostly by the people who were there. After an overview from Uncle Bob, it moves from Colossus and Grace Hopper through BASIC, Engelbart's 1968 demo, Unix, Xerox PARC and Lisp machines, then the home computer boom, free software and the open-sourcing of Netscape. Some are talks, some are films; all are ones HN keeps recommending.

videos.note: The opener and map: Uncle Bob tells the whole story from 1948 to today, which one HN commenter called a fascinating introduction to how hardware and languages evolved.
The start of the timeline, the wartime codebreaking machine at Bletchley Park, told with stories of the unsung engineers who built it.
Two minutes with the compiler pioneer herself, holding up a length of wire to make a nanosecond something you can see.
1964 at Dartmouth: Kemeny, Kurtz and their students invent BASIC and time-sharing, in what HN calls the definitive documentary on it.
1968: the mouse, hypertext, video calls and collaborative editing all shown in one sitting, which HN treats as essential viewing.
Unix and C from the source: Ken Thompson tells Kernighan how he wrote the Unix kernel in about three weeks, plus stories even Kernighan hadn't heard.
Bret Victor speaks as if it were 1973, a playful reminder of how many bold ideas from that era programming quietly dropped.
Xerox PARC in action: Dan Ingalls runs Smalltalk on a restored Alto, the live programming environment that shaped personal computing.
Lisp's high point, a whole computer built around the language; HN's go-to demo, and one commenter said it makes modern editors look like banging rocks together.
The early-80s home computer boom as a comic BBC drama about Sinclair versus Acorn, the rivalry that eventually produced ARM.
The free software story from Stallman and GNU to Torvalds and Linux, the standard documentary HN points to for the backstory.
A fitting close where the web and open source meet: Netscape engineers race to release the Mozilla source in 1998, filmed from inside the company.

title: Lectures worth a weekend
pitch: The recorded lectures Hacker News keeps telling people to watch: Feynman, SICP, Strang, Sapolsky, Sandel and other great teachers, one opening lecture from each.
intro: These are the university lectures and classic talks that HN commenters recommend again and again, often with the words 'drop what you're doing.' Each entry is a single lecture, usually the first of a full course, so you can sample a great teacher and keep going if it clicks. The list opens with Feynman, moves through physics, math, computing and machine learning, then turns to people, ethics and writing.

videos.note: The first of Feynman's 1964 Cornell Messenger Lectures, building from planetary motion to what a physical law is, clear enough that commenters say no formal training is needed.
J.N. Shive's Bell Labs wave machine demonstration, which HN calls the best introduction to waves of any sort, done with a contraption rather than equations.
Gilbert Strang's opening lecture on the geometry of linear equations, HN's default answer to how to learn linear algebra properly.
Abelson opens SICP by arguing that computer science is not about computers, the lecture one commenter says turned them from a UX designer into a programmer.
Andrew Ng's first CS229 lecture, recommended on HN as the original and more rigorous version of the course that taught a generation machine learning.
The AlphaGo lead's introduction to reinforcement learning, praised for clear explanations that pair well with Sutton and Barto's textbook.
Robert Sapolsky's first lecture on how genes, hormones and environment shape behavior, a series HN commenters keep calling the best course they have ever taken.
Michael Sandel opens his Harvard ethics course with the trolley problem and a hall full of students arguing, a series HN says everyone should watch.
Larry McEnerney's session on writing for what readers value, which many HN users say changed how they write well beyond academia.

title: Documentaries HN loves
pitch: Long-form documentaries Hacker News recommends for a slow evening: AlphaGo, Connections, Aaron Swartz, Adam Curtis and more, across tech, science, history and people.
intro: Feature-length and long-form documentaries that HN commenters recommend to each other, most of them an hour or more. It opens with the most welcoming of the lot, then moves through the history of computing and the hacker world, on to stories of science and the people behind it, and ends with films about how ideas spread and how societies fall. Pick one, settle in.

videos.note: The story of DeepMind's 2016 match against Lee Sedol works for technical and non-technical viewers alike, and one commenter calls it a timeless classic.
James Burke's 1978 opener starts with the 1965 New York blackout to show how fragile our interlocking technology is, and HN brings it up in every blackout thread.
The life of Aaron Swartz and the prosecution that ended it, which commenters call a must-watch for anyone who belongs to hacker culture.
WIRED's tour of Shenzhen's prototyping markets and copycat factories, the film HN links whenever hardware startups and fast manufacturing come up.
Veritasium's account of Shuji Nakamura's stubborn pursuit of the blue LED, which HN enjoys as a story of persistence against the consensus.
The first part of BobbyBroccoli's series on Jan Hendrik Schon's Bell Labs fraud, the film HN cites whenever research misconduct comes up.
Fredrik Knudsen's heartbreaking portrait of Terry Davis, his operating system and his illness, regarded on HN as the definitive account.
Adam Curtis traces how Freud's ideas and Edward Bernays's public relations shaped consumer culture, which one commenter says finally explained the why of American society.
Dan Olson's compassionate essay on how people fall into flat earth and wider conspiracy thinking, called by HN commenters the best documentary on the subject.
Fall of Civilizations on how a connected Mediterranean world came apart around 1100 BC, a long view to end on after Burke's fragile networks at the start.

title: How things are made
pitch: Factory tours and manufacturing explainers that give you the "how is this even made" feeling, from a soda can to EUV chip machines and rocket plants.
intro: HN loves watching things being made, and these are the videos it recommends most often. The list starts with everyday objects, moves to the craft and machines behind precision and heavy metalwork, then tours car and circuit board factories, then the light source inside a chipmaking machine, and finishes inside two rocket factories. Each one leaves you a bit more amazed by ordinary manufactured things.

videos.note: A welcoming eleven-minute start: Bill Hammack explains every detail of the humble soda can, and HN links it whenever cans or good design come up.
A designer tries to make a toaster from mined ore and homemade plastic, a short lesson in how much industry a cheap object depends on.
A quiet, mesmerizing record of one craftsman hand-making a nixie tube from glassblowing to vacuum, the kind of detail commenters say you almost never get to see.
Where precision itself comes from: how flat surfaces, lathes and measuring tools were built up from nothing, which HN calls a half hour well spent.
From the same channel, the Cold War presses that forge aircraft and turbine parts, often cited in HN threads about gigacasting and huge machines.
Destin Sandlin tours a progressive stamping plant and the tooling behind it, part of his series on what US manufacturing has lost.
A full tour of a car being built almost entirely by robots, with a carbon-fiber body that one commenter said looked like technology from the future.
Strange Parts walks through every step at JLCPCB, the factory behind many hobbyists' cheap circuit boards, and HN calls it the best look inside a modern PCB fab.
Then the hardest part of all: lasers firing twice at falling tin droplets to make the light for modern chips, explained in seventeen astonishing minutes.
ULA's CEO walks Destin through friction stir welding and huge milled rocket skins, a rare look inside a working rocket plant.
To finish, a walk around SpaceX's Starship factory, which HN quotes mainly for the engineering process Musk lays out, such as deleting requirements that should not exist.

title: Security war stories
pitch: Real hacks, cons and breaches, told by the people who pulled them off or tracked them down. From a KGB spy hunt in 1986 to the xz backdoor that nearly reached every Linux server.
intro: These are stories, not tutorials: people who broke into wallets, buildings and elevators, investigators who took apart Stuxnet and Mt. Gox, and the opsec mistakes that got hackers arrested. It opens with a single tense break-in, moves through cons and physical intrusion, then malware and crime, and ends with the near-miss supply chain attack of 2024. Most are conference talks that HN keeps linking because they are a pleasure to watch.

videos.note: A gripping opener: Joe Grand spends three months glitching a Trezor wallet, knowing he gets only one real chance to recover the $2 million inside.
The original hacker detective story: Cliff Stoll follows a 75-cent accounting error at Berkeley Lab all the way to a KGB-linked intruder, re-enacted by the people involved.
The real man behind Catch Me If You Can shows that social engineering predates computers, and HN still repeats his advice on credit cards and fraud.
Jim Browning turns a tech support scammer's connection back on them and ends up watching the call centre through its own CCTV.
A short, funny DEF CON talk in which a cheap eBay coffee order pulls a researcher into the world of stolen cards and reshipping fraud.
Deviant Ollam shows how professional break-in teams get through doors with a bit of wire and some confidence, and why physical security is so often the weak link.
HN's go-to link whenever elevators come up: two hours on how they work and how to get one to take you where you are not allowed, which commenters say they watched in one sitting.
An 11-minute account of how Langner's team worked out that Stuxnet was a state-built weapon aimed at industrial controllers, and a good primer for the next talk.
The first-hand version from Microsoft's analyst, which HN calls the definitive walk through each of Stuxnet's zero-days.
The investigator who traced Mt. Gox's missing bitcoins explains what actually happened, in what HN calls the clearest and most even-handed account of the collapse.
The Grugq goes through hacker indictments to show how people who thought they were careful got caught, and HN treats it as the essential opsec talk.
Silk Road and other darknet busts, case by case, showing that the operators' own mistakes mattered far more than any flaw in Tor.
To close, Veritasium's documentary on the xz backdoor: an attacker who spent years earning a maintainer's trust and very nearly compromised SSH across Linux.

title: Systems and databases
pitch: The deep technical talks HN recommends for learning how real systems work: databases, consensus, testing distributed code, performance and keeping production running.
intro: These are the talks Hacker News points to when someone wants to know how real systems work underneath. It opens with a friendly story about scaling Dropbox. Then it moves through databases and storage, consensus and distributed data, running at scale, and performance. It ends with what happens when systems fail and how the people running them cope.

videos.note: A good way in: a Dropbox engineer frankly walks through growing the service from nothing to millions of users, schema decisions included, and one commenter found it one of the most riveting things ever.
The creator of the world's most widely used database explains where SQLite fits, how it is tested and why it gets long-term support, with an energy commenters enjoy as much as the content.
Rick Houlihan's dense session is HN's go-to for learning to design data around access patterns, and a clear overview of how NoSQL thinking differs from SQL.
Kleppmann reframes a database as a log of immutable facts with caches and indexes derived from it, the talk commenters say changed how they think about derived data.
On to consensus: John Ousterhout's clear walkthrough of Paxos and Multi-Paxos, recorded for the Raft study and best watched alongside its Raft companion lecture.
When replicas disagree instead of agreeing on one leader, this approachable primer on operational transformation and CRDTs is what HN keeps linking in local-first threads.
FoundationDB ran its whole database inside a simulator with injected faults to find rare bugs, and HN treats this as the defining talk on simulation testing.
Rick Reed shows how a handful of engineers ran WhatsApp's message load on FreeBSD and Erlang, with real server counts and the bottlenecks they fixed.
Moving down to the physical layer, Hamilton tours how AWS builds its networking, power and custom silicon, which HN considers the best look inside a cloud provider.
Performance at the scale of one data structure: the step-by-step story of SwissTable, the design that now sits behind Abseil, Rust's HashMap and Go's maps.
Before trusting any benchmark, learn why averages mislead and what coordinated omission is; some commenters call this talk life-changing.
Cantrill recounts the day a mistyped command rebooted a whole Joyent datacenter, which HN remembers as the best postmortem it has seen, and a funny one.

title: Hidden gems
pitch: Videos Hacker News loves that YouTube has barely noticed, most with well under 50,000 views. Physics, music, spacecraft, genetics, energy and software history.
intro: Every video here has a loyal following on Hacker News and a small audience everywhere else. The subjects range widely on purpose, so expect to find at least one you would never have searched for. It starts with a one-minute demo and short talks, and ends with longer evening-length pieces.

videos.note: A one-minute opener: a bouncing oil droplet makes an interference pattern, and HN shares it to help people build intuition about wave-particle duality.
A short talk from a blind developer that lets you hear a screen reader at full speed, and at one point it shows how inaccessible Hacker News itself is.
Alan Kay honors Ted Nelson on a revived 1970s Smalltalk system, and HN keeps returning to it to show how programmable software from that era was.
Nineteen minutes on why complex systems run close to failure, which one HN commenter calls one of the most important talks they have seen.
Chris Ford builds from a single sine wave up to a Bach canon in code, and several HN readers say it was the talk that made music theory click.
The most-recommended video under 50k views: Flask's creator explains why Python is so hard to speed up, and people who build JITs keep recommending it on HN.
A Voyager team engineer tells how they diagnosed and patched a 1970s spacecraft from 15 billion miles away, which HN calls a great blind-debugging story.
Physicist Geoffrey West on the scaling laws that govern organisms, cities and companies, recommended on HN as an accessible doorway to the subject.
A physician treats genetic diseases as exploits in the human genome, a DEF CON talk that some HN readers say convinced them to keep their DNA out of databases.
Meredith Patterson and Sergey Bratus explain why messy input formats keep software insecure, which HN regards as the standard introduction to LANGSEC.
Vaclav Smil uses data on how slowly past energy transitions happened, and HN often links it as a sober counterpoint to techno-optimism.
A mathematician juggles while explaining the notation that led to new juggling patterns, an entertaining math lecture HN readers remember fondly.
Jason Scott recounts recovering the Prince of Persia source code from decaying floppies with its author, and HN treats it as a favorite example of digital archaeology.

title: A comedy break for programmers
pitch: The sketches, parodies and absurd talks that Hacker News threads link for a laugh, from meetings with impossible requirements to a Turing machine built in PowerPoint.
intro: These are the funny videos Hacker News commenters keep linking when a thread gets a little too true: office sketches, tech-hype parodies, deadpan fake research and one famously funny keynote. Most are under ten minutes. The list starts with workplace humor, moves through hype and programming culture, and ends with absurd talks, closing on the longest one.

videos.note: The obvious opener: an engineer asked to draw seven red lines with blue ink, which HN posts whenever a thread turns to impossible requirements.
A Webby-winning classic about an outage call where sales and engineering talk straight past each other.
KRAZAM's three-minute tour of a hopelessly tangled backend, the go-to joke in any thread about architecture sprawl.
A second KRAZAM sketch, this one about Slack chimes and corporate life, which one commenter called so good it is painful to watch.
Kai Lentit's parody of scrum and sprint jargon, recommended because it looks a lot like agile at large companies.
The animated NoSQL-hype dialogue that still gets posted whenever someone promises a database will just scale.
Not meant as comedy, but HN loves this earnest Ericsson film showing hot code reloading, and you need it before the sequel.
The parody follow-up, with the Outlaw Techno Psychobitch take on OTP; one commenter shows both films to classes at Oxford.
Dylan Beattie sets 'We Didn't Start the Fire' to a list of real framework names, a fair joke about the churn in web development.
The Onion's MacBook Wheel, still HN's punchline whenever a device drops physical keys.
The original late-1970s technobabble parody, a minute of solemn engineering jargon that means nothing.
Will Stephen does the same thing for TED talks, spending six minutes saying nothing while sounding brilliant.
A deadpan SIGBOVIK result proving PowerPoint animations are Turing complete, which HN often names as one of the funniest talks it knows.
The long one to finish: James Mickens's keynote is both very funny and a serious warning about trusting machine learning, and HN keeps rewatching it.

title: Indistinguishable From Magic
pitch: From one transistor on a kitchen table to the tin-droplet lasers inside ASML's machines, then out to the people and countries fighting over the result.
intro: A guided trip down the chip stack. It starts with what a transistor is and with hobbyists who make them at home, goes through the modern fab and EUV lithography, and ends with the industry and the argument over whether Moore's Law is finished. The centerpiece is the HOPE talk HN has called the best introduction to chipmaking for more than ten years.

videos.note: Ben Eater's eleven-minute NPN explainer comes first because HN treats it as the starting point that leads on to logic gates and CPUs.
Jeri Ellsworth makes an NMOS transistor with a kiln, rust remover and eBay wafers, which shows each fab step at kitchen scale before the industrial version.
Five minutes on Sam Zeloof's garage fab making chips with around a thousand transistors; HN cites it as the proof that hobby chipmaking is real.
Branch Education's animated tour of deposition, lithography and etching gives you a map of the real fab before the long talk.
The centerpiece, with 19 HN recommenders: a HOPE talk that treats 22nm chipmaking as physics hacking, and the one HN keeps wishing someone would update.
Asianometry zooms in on the hardest part, where lasers hit falling tin droplets twice to make 13.5nm light, and it is the link HN reaches for whenever ASML comes up.
Veritasium's 55-minute look at the whole EUV machine, from mirrors to supply chain, which one HN commenter said turned deep magic into something understandable.
A short reality check: der8auer puts Intel 14nm and AMD 7nm under an electron microscope and shows that node names are marketing labels.
After the machines come the people: TSMC's founder explains how he invented the pure-play foundry model, interviewed in 2007 by the Nvidia CEO who became his biggest customer.
A 38C3 talk that pulls the technical story into geopolitics, about why EUV and its supply chain now matter to governments.
The closer is the talk HN cites in every Moore's Law argument, where Keller lays out the overlapping curves he thinks keep scaling going.

title: Mechanical Sympathy
pitch: Why your fast computer runs slow code, and what the people who write fast code know about caches, data layout and measurement.
intro: A path through the performance talks Hacker News keeps linking whenever someone asks why software got slow. It starts with mindset (don't do needless work), moves to the memory hierarchy and data-oriented design, then to measuring honestly, and ends with two console war stories where all of it pays off.

videos.note: An 18-minute opener that separates real optimization from 'non-pessimization', the idea HN cites most often to explain why modern software is slow.
Matthias Wandel benchmarks old and new PCs and finds branchy code barely got faster in 15 years, which is why the rest of this list matters.
The plain explanation of cache levels and associativity that HN points to for why memory layout beats pointer chasing.
With the cache model in hand, Acton's blunt argument that a program's job is transforming data lands much harder; it is HN's default data-oriented design talk.
The practical follow-up to Acton: struct-of-arrays and compact layouts applied to a real compiler, with measured wins in Zig.
One data structure redesigned around the cache, step by step; HN calls it the definitive explanation of SwissTable, now behind Rust's and Go's maps.
Proof this is not just a C++ story: a generalist's tour of pipelining and cache effects that HN liked for its humor and hardware knowledge.
The turn from making things fast to knowing whether they are; commenters call the coordinated omission material life changing.
Shows that code layout alone can swamp your optimization, and offers causal profiling as the fix; HN's standard answer to mysterious benchmark swings.
Everything above applied to a real console: Kaze finds bus contention and easy wins that make Mario 64 render several times faster.
The closer and the most-recommended war story here: Andy Gavin overwriting Sony's own library code in RAM to make the game fit.

title: Things You Never Look At
pitch: Doors, plugs, cans, toasters and turn signals, explained by people who obviously love them. Short design essays about everyday objects.
intro: A relaxed list for a slow afternoon, made from the design explainers HN links whenever someone says 'there is a great video about this'. It starts with short pieces on sound and doors, moves to manufactured objects and the appliances that were better in the past, and widens out to design failures that cost lives or miss their users. It ends with Saul Bass pitching a logo, which HN holds up as how to present design.

videos.note: A one-minute opener on why backup alarms switched to white noise: it is easier to tell where the sound comes from.
The short, canonical explainer of the Norman door, which introduces the idea of affordances that the rest of the list relies on.
The video HN posts every time plugs come up: fuses, shutters, and safety built into the shape.
Bill Hammack explains why a can is shaped the way it is, HN's standard example of a well-designed mass-produced object.
An old microwave with a steam sensor, cited in many HN threads as proof that older appliances could be smarter.
More appliance nostalgia: why a 1940s Sunbeam toaster still sets the standard.
Paired with the previous video: building one cheap toaster from ore and oil shows how much industry a simple object depends on.
A calm tour of seven-segment displays and stranger alternatives that only appear in old patents.
The tone gets serious: a styling trend, tall truck hoods, tied directly to pedestrian deaths.
Widens the frame to expert blindness, meaning designs that only work in the culture they were made for.
Roman Mars's five rules for flags, which HN reuses for logos and branding.
It ends with the 1969 pitch film HN considers a masterclass in explaining and selling a design.

title: Debugging at a Distance
pitch: From the Apollo Guidance Computer's 1202 alarms to patching Voyager 1's memory from 15 billion miles away: the hardest remote debugging jobs ever done, told by the people who did them or who rebuilt the hardware.
intro: Hacker News loves a war story about software you can't touch, and spacecraft are the most extreme case. This playlist runs roughly in order of history: two ways into the Apollo Guidance Computer, the restoration of a real one, then Voyager's 1970s computers, a Lisp REPL on Deep Space 1, a visit to the antenna that still talks to Voyager, and the 2023 rescue of Voyager 1. It ends with the photo Voyager took on its way out.

videos.note: The way in: Robert Wills explains the AGC and then walks through the Apollo 11 landing step by step, 1202 alarms included, and HN keeps calling it mandatory viewing.
Once the landing story makes sense, Steil and Hessmann go through the whole machine layer by layer, from hardware to OS to mission software, which commenters call the most complete AGC talk there is.
Now you see the real thing: CuriousMarc and Mike Stewart open a privately owned AGC in a Houston hotel-room lab, the first episode of a series HN recommends whole.
Thirty episodes later, the team builds a reader to recover lost programs from core rope memory, which a commenter calls the deepest dive on rope ROM anywhere.
A maker interlude before Voyager: Applied Science rebuilds the astronauts' electroluminescent display panel from scratch, so you see the other end of the AGC too.
Moves from 1969 to 1977: a Strange Loop tour of the three computer systems that still fly Voyager, and why they have lasted so long.
Ron Garret's first-hand account of finding a race condition in Lisp on Deep Space 1 through a live REPL in 1999, which HN cites in nearly every thread about remote REPLs.
Before the rescue story, see the other end of the link: EEVblog's Dave Jones tours the 70m DSS-43 dish in Canberra with its operations supervisor.
Inside the control room, with live spectrum displays of a signal that left the spacecraft about a day earlier.
A short, lively version of the 2023 telemetry failure from someone on the team, covering 1970s architecture and documentation that had gone missing.
The full engineering version for flight-software people: no simulator, a failed memory chip, and code relocated around it, which one commenter called mind-blowing reverse engineering.
The closer: Voyager 1 took this photo of Earth in 1990 on its way out, and HN commenters say they rewatch Sagan's three minutes about it every so often.

title: Brass Brains: Computing With Gears
pitch: Before transistors, people did calculus with gears, cams and water. This walks from one differential gear to the machines that aimed battleships, predicted tides and ran a model economy.
intro: Hacker News keeps returning to one idea: a computer does not need electricity. This playlist starts with the smallest building block, a differential gear that adds two rotations, then shows those parts combined into Navy fire-control computers. From there it goes back through Antikythera, Babbage and Kelvin's tide machines, out to mechanical oddities, and ends with the case that analog computing may come back for AI.

videos.note: Start with the 1937 GM film HN calls a marvel of teaching: the differential it explains is the adding unit every later machine here relies on.
The 1953 Navy training film, the full-length upload HN prefers, shows how shafts, cams and differentials put together solve firing equations; several commenters admit rewatching it many times.
Once the parts make sense, Veritasium supplies the history, from Antikythera to Kelvin's tide-predicting machines.
Clickspring's opening episode on rebuilding the oldest known gear computer by hand, using only methods the Greeks could plausibly have had.
Doron Swade, who led the team that finally built Difference Engine No. 2, tells the Babbage story; HN points to the section around minute 36 on Ada Lovelace.
Bill Hammack's short series on Michelson's harmonic analyzer, which does Fourier analysis with springs and levers, is what HN links whenever Fourier series come up.
Three minutes of slow motion showing an office typewriter with a fully mechanical digital-to-analog converter inside.
The pocket-sized Curta, here as a scaled-up 3D-printed replica, so you can see the stepped drum that the original hides.
A teardown of a working Cold War navigation computer, for anyone who wants to see the cams and gears from the Navy film in real hardware.
A change of medium: Bill Phillips' machine models a national economy with water flowing through tanks and valves.
Matthias Wandel's wooden binary adder moves from analog to digital logic, and HN says it inspired at least one commercial marble computer.
Steve Mould turns the analogy around and builds resistors, capacitors and transistors from chains and sprockets.
It ends where HN threads usually end up, with the argument that continuous computation could return for neural-network inference.

title: Objects on Trial
pitch: The OOP argument HN has been having for fifteen years, staged as a trial: the defense, the prosecution, the founder's testimony, and a two-hour closing statement.
intro: Few topics start longer HN threads than object-oriented programming. This list lets each side make its best case in order: first the people who make objects work, then the critics, then Alan Kay on what he actually meant, and finally Casey Muratori's history of how we got here. Watch it in order and decide for yourself.

videos.note: The defense opens with its strongest witness: Metz turns ugly conditionals into small objects, and HN quotes her 'duplication is cheaper than the wrong abstraction' more than anything else here.
Misko Hevery's 2008 case for replacing if and switch statements with polymorphism, the textbook OO move the prosecution will later attack.
Uncle Bob's argument for craftsmanship as an ethical duty; HN fans say the lecture is better than the book, and it is the style several later critics take aim at.
The prosecution starts gently: Jack Diederich deletes needless Python classes, and several HN commenters say this talk changed how they write code.
Brian Will's full indictment that encapsulation is mostly illusory, HN's go-to anti-OOP video with 13 recommenders.
The evidence phase: four short programs, including Uncle Bob-style Java, rewritten to show how objects scatter state.
A different charge, performance: Muratori benchmarks clean-code polymorphism against plain code, and it now shows up in every SOLID debate on HN.
A third way: Seemann argues functional design gives you the OO best practices for free, with a pure core and an impure shell.
The witness everyone cites: Kay on biological cells and why he thought objects would help software scale, which looks nothing like the classes on trial so far.
Erlang's creator questions Kay about message passing, and HN uses this conversation to argue that Erlang processes are closer to Kay's objects than Java is.
The two-hour closing argument, a source-based history back to the 1960s; HN loved the research and still disputes its account of Kay, so it makes a good end to the debate.

title: Before It Worked
pitch: AI history told through talks recorded before the field took off, from the 1973 debate that helped start an AI winter to the 2017 speech that called the boom alchemy.
intro: Most AI videos on HN are about what works now. This playlist goes back to the talks HN kept linking while neural nets were still a fringe bet: the debates, the demos and the pioneers explaining ideas almost nobody used yet. It runs in chronological order, from 1973 to 2017. The last two talks are critiques from people inside the field.

videos.note: The full 1973 BBC debate in which Lighthill argues against McCarthy and Michie, the argument that came before the first AI winter, with vintage footage of the Freddy robot.
In 1985 Feynman notes how hard it is to name anything a computer will never do, and HN still quotes that point in AGI arguments.
Four minutes of evolved block creatures from 1994, which HN cites as the classic example of optimization exploiting simulator bugs.
Norvig's 2007 case that more data beats cleverer models, the statistical approach that came before deep learning took over.
Andrew Ng in 2011 showing networks learn their own features from unlabeled data, a talk nine HN commenters recommended over two years as the simple overview of the coming wave.
A 2011 vision demo that learns as it tracks, which HN remembers as primitive but effective and a reminder that pre-deep-learning methods could already impress.
Hinton in 2012 explains dropout through sexual reproduction and spiking neurons, which HN calls a simple, elegant account of the technique.
Microsoft's 2012 live demo turning English speech into Chinese in the speaker's own voice, one of the first public signs that deep nets had arrived.
A 2015 look inside a convnet watching a live camera, with individual units lighting up for faces and text.
Once convnets had won, Hinton came back to argue that pooling is a mistake and to pitch capsules instead.
The ending: the field's most-quoted critique of itself, which argues that machine learning had become alchemy just as it started to work.

title: How to Count a Vote
pitch: Voting is an algorithm, and HN argues about it like one. From why first-past-the-post breeds two parties, through Arrow's theorem and score voting, to gerrymandering and why paper ballots still beat computers.
intro: Every election thread on Hacker News turns into a voting theory seminar, and these are the videos commenters keep linking. The order is a short course: first the problem with plurality voting, then the alternatives and their failure modes, then the math that says no system is perfect, then how district maps and ballot counting can be gamed. Most are under 15 minutes.

videos.note: Starts with the problem: HN's default explainer of how first-past-the-post pushes any country toward two parties.
Primer's simulated voters run plurality, ranked choice and approval side by side, so you see each system's behavior instead of taking it on faith.
A three-minute warning before you fall for ranked choice: the clip HN posts to show that instant runoff can still punish voters for ranking their favorite first.
Veritasium turns the specific flaws into a general result, walking through Arrow's theorem and why every ranked method gives something up.
Picks up right where Arrow leaves off, showing how score voting sidesteps the theorem by having voters rate candidates instead of ranking them.
A little-watched gem: colored win regions across a 2D political space make the case for cardinal methods like STAR better than any argument could.
Moves from picking one winner to filling a legislature, with HN's standard link for single transferable vote and why incumbents avoid it.
Even a perfect ballot fails if the map is rigged: AlphaPhoenix uses Monte Carlo search to draw North Carolina districts fair and foul.
A brief detour into a more radical idea HN keeps returning to: lending your vote to someone you trust, and taking it back when you like.
Then the counting itself: Tom Scott's argument, linked in nearly every e-voting thread, that software attacks scale in ways attacks on paper cannot.
The cryptographer's reply: Ron Rivest explains how a receipt can prove your vote was counted without letting you prove to anyone how you voted.
Ends with auditing results: Matt Parker shows when Benford's Law can catch fraud and why it does not apply to precinct totals.

title: Speedrunners Are Reverse Engineers
pitch: From one Mario Kart shortcut to running Flappy Bird inside Super Mario World with only a controller: how players took their games apart.
intro: HN likes speedrunning less as a sport than as people reverse engineering a game in public. This list starts with an easy way into speedrunning history, then moves to collision physics, then to arbitrary code execution done with controller inputs, then to cracking random number generators. It ends with a five-hour history for anyone who has stopped resisting.

videos.note: The opener: one HN commenter says this is the video that made them care about speedrunning, told as a story of record holders and discoveries.
Before breaking a game you need its rules, and this walkthrough of Mario 64's triangle collision code is the textbook for that.
The famous 'half an A press' video, which HN describes as insanely complicated and surprisingly lucid, built on those collision rules.
Moving from physics to memory: an animated, assembly-level explanation of how an item glitch makes the SNES jump to the ending.
The same exploit done by a human on a real console, a moment HN remembers as a trick escaping tool-assisted runs.
SethBling types an entire new game into memory with a controller, HN's go-to example of arbitrary code execution through gameplay.
The Game Boy version of the idea, taken so far that Pokemon Yellow ends up running other programs.
An hour of a robot at a live event pushing video and chat through controller ports, which HN calls a reliably great GDQ watch.
A turn to randomness: a community reverse engineers Wind Waker's RNG to win the Sploosh Kaboom minigame every time.
RNG cracking on a larger scale, a distributed search through world seeds that one HN commenter promises will blow your mind.
The same probability math pointed at a cheater, which Matt Parker turns into a lesson HN liked on negligible probabilities.
The five-hour finale for those now hooked, chronicling years of SM64 exploit discovery that HN calls an insane amount of knowledge.

title: Cheating the Hardware
pitch: How game developers got around tiny RAM, few colors and slow disks, from Asteroids to Crash Bandicoot, in roughly chronological order.
intro: HN never gets tired of stories about game developers beating hardware that should not have been able to run their game. This playlist goes in rough order of the hardware: vector monitors, CGA, the Apple II, 8-bit palettes, the Game Boy, the 90s software renderers, the PlayStation and N64. It ends with modern programmers who go back to old consoles by choice.

videos.note: A seven-minute primer on sprites, attribute grids and palettes that gives you the vocabulary for everything after it.
Before pixels were cheap, Asteroids and Tempest drew with an electron beam, and HN's pick for how that vector hardware worked is this one.
The 1981 IBM PC's four-color mode turns out to give more colors on a composite monitor, and HN praises it for showing how developers took advantage of the smeared signal.
Jordan Mechner on rotoscoped animation and memory tricks on a dying platform, which HN calls essential viewing for game history.
The highest-scored video in game history on HN: LucasArts artist Mark Ferrari animating whole scenes with nothing but palette cycling.
Michael Steil explains nearly the whole handheld in an hour, and HN tells would-be emulator authors to watch it first.
Hecker, Barrett and others tell the oral history of how 90s PCs drew textured 3D with no GPU, a rarely watched first-hand account.
A three-minute anecdote about a crash handler that sends a CPU fault to the level select, a small example of the kind of defensive engineering the next video relies on.
The centerpiece and one of HN's most recommended dev stories: Andy Gavin overwriting Sony's own libraries in RAM to make room for his game.
The most famous single trick of the era, 0x5f3759df, explained clearly enough that HN commenters say it finally made sense.
A modern coda: Kaze Emanuar finds bus contention and other N64 bottlenecks and makes Mario 64 render up to six times faster on real hardware.
It ends in 2018 with a studio that chose the NES's limits on purpose, the video HN links whenever someone asks how old games were so small.

title: Everything Is Circles
pitch: One idea, the Fourier transform, followed from Homer Simpson drawn in epicycles to JPEG, digital audio, radio, lenses and the uncertainty principle.
intro: HN keeps recommending the same handful of Fourier explainers, and together they cover a lot of engineering. This list starts with the intuition, follows the algorithm and its Cold War history, then visits the places it quietly runs: images, audio, radio and optics. It ends with the result that links it to quantum physics.

videos.note: A three-minute hook: enough epicycles can trace Homer Simpson's face, which HN uses both to explain Fourier series and to warn about overfitting.
HN's default first explanation, the one many commenters say finally made the transform make sense.
Michelson's gear-driven harmonic analyzer computed Fourier series a century ago; the first of Bill Hammack's four short episodes.
Derives the FFT from polynomial multiplication; one commenter rewatches it every six months.
The FFT's backstory in nuclear test detection and Cold War politics, the human side of the algorithm from the video before.
The first everyday use: the cosine transform inside every JPEG, explained clearly enough that several commenters say they finally understood the DCT.
Sampling and the frequency domain on real bench gear, the gold-standard answer HN gives to audiophile stair-step myths.
Radio's central trick, shifting signals between frequencies by mixing them, explained by Technology Connections in twelve minutes.
A plain lens computes a Fourier transform at the speed of light, shown with a DLP projector doing pattern recognition.
The closer: uncertainty is a property of waves, not of measurement, which ties everything above to quantum mechanics.

title: Biology for Programmers
pitch: Cells as nanoscale machine shops, bioelectric networks that store body plans, genetic diseases treated as exploits, and a Lisp compiler for designing molecules. Biology seen the way HN sees it: as the strangest codebase there is.
intro: HN commenters keep finding biology through computing: Sussman's talk on how we don't know how to compute, Levin's NeurIPS talk, a DEF CON talk on hacking the genome. This playlist starts with that framing, shows you the molecular machinery in animation, moves to Levin's idea that tissues compute shape, then to security, static analysis and DIY gene therapy, and ends with the Lisp hacker designing molecules.

videos.note: The framing: Sussman sets biology's robustness against how brittle our programs are, and one commenter says it made them question what programming is.
Now look at the hardware: Drew Berry's accurate animations of DNA replication, which left one commenter in awe of the trillions of protein machines inside us.
Seven minutes of the same molecular machinery with no narration, jostling and mechanical, and the clip HN posts most often to show it.
Three minutes on the ribosome reading codons and assembling a protein, the clip HN posted widely in the mRNA-vaccine threads.
The power supply: proton pumps and ATP synthase as an actual rotary motor, which commenters share as the clearest example of nanomachines in cells.
Evolution as a search algorithm you can watch, as bacteria work their way across rising antibiotic doses in days.
Up from molecules to tissues: Levin's 20-minute introduction to the bioelectric layer, with two-headed worms and xenobots.
The full version given to an ML audience, and the talk that introduced many HN readers to Levin's view of cell collectives as computers that store pattern memories.
The security engineer's view: genetic diseases as known exploits, a talk that convinced several commenters to keep their DNA out of databases.
Static analysis and precision medicine in one talk, built on Might's search for his son's diagnosis, which commenters call a must-see.
Biology as a garage hack: a home-made AAV gene therapy tested on the host himself, the example HN keeps citing in biohacking threads.
The closer: a chemist writes his own Lisp compiler to design molecules, and commenters dare anyone to watch it and not be impressed.

title: Who Watches the Silicon?
pitch: Your threat model probably stops at the OS. These talks go below it: undocumented CPU instructions, hidden coprocessors, malicious USB firmware, and implants on motherboards.
intro: A descent through the layers of a computer you cannot see or audit, ordered from the peripherals inward to the CPU, its secret co-processors and firmware, then out to the board and the supply chain. Most of these are HN gems with modest view counts, and HN brings them up whenever Intel ME, backdoors or hardware trust come up. It ends with the defender's view: how Microsoft built a console meant to survive people with soldering irons.

videos.note: A five-minute Princeton demo that encryption keys survive in DRAM after power-off, a quick first sign that the hardware doesn't behave the way you assume.
Nohl and Lell reprogram USB controller firmware to impersonate other devices, which HN treats as the standard reference for why any USB stick is a computer you don't control.
Christopher Domas fuzzes the processor itself with Sandsifter and finds undocumented instructions; HN calls it easy to follow and entertaining.
The follow-up: a hidden alternate instruction set on a real x86 chip that bypasses privilege rings, the talk HN brings up in every CPU-backdoor thread.
Rutkowska steps back from single bugs to ask whether an x86 laptop with Intel ME can be trusted at all, and one HN commenter labeled it essential.
Google's Minnich explains UEFI as a large closed attack surface and why his team wanted to replace it with Linux, the firmware talk HN keeps linking.
Timothy Roscoe zooms out to show how much of a modern SoC runs below and beside Linux, which HN found revelatory and which explains why the earlier talks were possible.
Leaving the chip for the board: bunnie gives a measured, technical look at how realistic a hidden implant is, written in the wake of the Supermicro story.
Laurie and Franken show how to take a chip's package off and read its ROM from the die, the practical answer to whether you can just look inside.
bunnie's harder conclusion is that checking hardware destroys it, so even open designs leave a time-of-check/time-of-use gap, and he sketches what might narrow it.
The defender gets the last word: a mostly successful design, built to make any hardware attack cost more than buying the games, and HN's standard reference for it.

title: How Things Fall Over
pitch: Deleted databases, a nuclear accident, a datacenter rebooted by one typo, and the ideas from safety science that explain why all of it was normal.
intro: HN's reading list for the day after an outage. It opens with short, funny disaster stories, moves into detailed incident accounts and the craft of debugging under pressure, then to designs that limit the damage. It ends with Richard Cook's two short Velocity talks, which several commenters say they rewatch every few months.

videos.note: Two minutes to start: Pixar nearly lost a film to one command and was saved by a home-computer backup, a cautionary tale HN tells to anyone in storage or SRE.
Kevin Fang's comic but accurate retelling of GitLab's 2017 incident, where every backup layer failed in turn, which HN prescribes for a bad ops day.
A rescue engineer's first-hand account of a failure that was organizational, not technical: nobody owned the whole site.
A minute-by-minute account of a nuclear accident, which HN uses to push back whenever an outage gets blamed on human error.
The postmortem HN rates above almost every written one: a mistyped command reboots a whole Joyent datacenter, and Cantrill walks through what came after.
A calmer counterpart on method (form hypotheses, try to falsify them, write everything down), which several commenters say changed how they debug.
Cantrill again, on the rare failures (firmware, disks, opaque hardware) that keep turning out to be the real cause, a talk HN calls entertaining and sobering.
Moving from response to design: cell-based architecture and shuffle sharding, which HN links whenever someone asks how to contain an outage.
Erlang's creator makes the case for letting things crash and recover, a conceptual talk rather than a code-heavy one.
The most demanding answer here: TigerBeetle's method of assertions, up-front design and deterministic simulation for software meant to be defect-free.
A patient-safety physician explains to ops engineers why complex systems always run partly broken, and one HN commenter rewatches it every couple of months.
The capstone, in 19 minutes: Cook's model of pressures pushing a system toward the edge of failure, which one commenter called among the most important talks they had seen.

title: Small, Profitable, Nobody's Unicorn
pitch: The talks HN sends to anyone who wants a business rather than a rocket ship: DHH's 2008 heresy, Jason Cohen's bootstrapping playbook, Maciej on barely succeeding, and a game studio that has stayed alive since 1994.
intro: Hacker News is funded by a startup accelerator, yet a large share of its readers don't want venture capital, and these are the talks they pass around. It opens on luck and cheap experiments, then gets to the 2008 argument for charging customers, then practical advice on pricing, contracts and solo shipping. It ends with people who have kept small, independent operations going for decades.

videos.note: Opens with how luck works: 72 odd side projects in one year, and HN's favorite answer to survivorship-bias success stories.
The founding text, given at Y Combinator's own event: charge money, stay small, ignore the exit, which founders still call career-changing.
The counterexample: AvE takes apart a venture-funded juicer and shows what unlimited money and no constraints look like in machined aluminum.
The Pinboard founder's dry case for aiming lower, and a gem HN found inspiring even though few have watched it.
DHH five years on, with the argument expanded: planning is guessing and constraints help you.
Five minutes of Clayton Christensen's milkshake story, the simplest tool here for working out what customers would actually pay for.
The practical core and the top-scoring video in the startup section: start from your own life and constraints, and work back to pricing and market.
The part bootstrappers forget: contracts, lawyers and collecting payment, which HN sends to every freelancer whose client won't pay.
The solo-maker version: a tour of many shipped projects and why being a generalist matters when nobody is paying for a team.
A funny cautionary tale about a joke app that got real users, and the support burden that came with them.
Long-run proof: Jeff Vogel has made a comfortable living from indie games since 1994, and HN calls the talk legendary.
Ends with the furthest version of the idea: Blender's creator on building world-class software without running it as a business at all.
